nameStory: The Wood Stork gets its name from its habit of roosting and nesting in wooded areas, particularly cypress swamps and other wetland forests. Unlike many other storks that prefer open grasslands, this species has a strong association with trees, making "wood" the perfect descriptor for North America's only breeding stork.
description: The Wood Stork is a large, impressive wading bird that stands about 3-4 feet tall with a wingspan reaching 5-6 feet across. Its body is mostly white with black flight feathers and tail, while its most distinctive feature is a featherless, dark gray head and neck that looks almost prehistoric. This is North America's only native stork species, and it's built for wading through shallow water to hunt fish and other aquatic prey.

idTips.label: Bald head and neck
idTips.description: The head and neck are completely bare of feathers, appearing dark gray and wrinkled like old leather - this naked appearance is unmistakable among large wading birds

idTips.label: Massive size
idTips.description: Much larger than herons or egrets, standing 3-4 feet tall with a heavy, robust build that makes other wading birds look delicate by comparison

idTips.label: Black and white plumage
idTips.description: Body appears bright white from a distance, but the wings show dramatic black flight feathers with a subtle greenish-purple sheen visible in good light

idTips.label: Thick, down-curved bill
idTips.description: Heavy, dark bill that curves slightly downward at the tip, much thicker and more substantial than the straight, pointed bills of herons

idTips.label: Soaring flight
idTips.description: Often seen soaring high overhead on broad wings with neck extended forward, looking like a small airplane compared to the tucked-neck flight of herons

habitat: In New England, Wood Storks are rare visitors typically found around large freshwater wetlands, coastal marshes, and tidal areas with shallow water. They prefer areas where fish concentrate, such as receding ponds, mudflats, or the edges of lakes and rivers. Most sightings occur near the coast or major river systems during migration periods.

seasonality.spring: Rare spring migrants may appear from April through May, often during warm weather patterns that bring southern species northward. Look for them in coastal areas and large wetlands.
seasonality.summer: Occasional summer visitors, particularly during hot, dry periods when they may wander north following food sources. Most active during early morning and late afternoon feeding times.
seasonality.fall: Peak time for New England sightings from August through October as birds disperse after breeding season. Young birds are more likely to wander far from traditional range.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in winter, with only exceptional records during unusually mild periods. Any winter sighting would be noteworthy for local birding communities.

funFact: Wood Storks hunt by touch rather than sight - they stick their partially open bill underwater and snap it shut in just 25 milliseconds when they feel a fish, making them one of the fastest-reacting animals in the world!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Great Blue Heron due to size, but remember that herons have feathered heads and necks, fly with their necks tucked back, and lack the distinctive bald, dark head of the Wood Stork. Think "bald head = stork" as your memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: Wood Storks were once endangered in the U.S. due to habitat loss in the Florida Everglades, but their status has improved to threatened as populations have grown and expanded northward. Any New England sighting represents the northern edge of this recovery success story.
compareHints: Wood Storks are the only members of their genus in the Americas and the only stork species that breeds in North America. Compared to other large wading birds like Great Blue Herons or Great Egrets, Wood Storks are bulkier, have the distinctive bald head, and show more dramatic black-and-white plumage contrast.
